78: Choosing the vehicle is the first decision that shapes everything else in this plan. In the United States we weigh two main options: a self-contained truck, where the kitchen and the engine share one chassis, and a towed trailer. A truck gives us full autonomy and a single unit to park, register and insure, while a trailer usually costs less up front and frees the tow vehicle for errands, but it is harder to maneuver and park in tight city lots. For a mid-sized urban concept we budget {{inv_vehiculo}} for a used truck in sound mechanical condition and {{inv_adaptacion}} for the build-out and wrap, which includes the plumbing, electrical work, ventilation and finishes the health department will want to see on the plans. The choice between new and used comes down to warranty against depreciation already absorbed by someone else. With a moderate startup budget, our recommendation is a used vehicle that a mechanic has inspected before we sign, plus a full kitchen build-out designed around our own menu rather than a previous owner's.
79: The kitchen has to be sized carefully so that it does not become a bottleneck at the lunch rush. A typical street-food setup needs a professional flat-top griddle, a fryer with a reliable thermostat, a refrigerated prep table, a handwashing sink and a ventilation hood that meets local fire code. In our plan, kitchen and refrigeration equipment come to {{inv_equipo_cocina}}. The generator is the item first-time owners underestimate most: it has to carry every appliance at once, run quietly enough for events and last a full service day on a single fill. We budget {{inv_generador}} for it. Whether we buy new or reconditioned equipment, we favor commercial-grade, NSF-listed pieces, because health inspectors tend to look for them and they hold up to a daily cycle of loading, driving and cleaning.
80: Our daily routine determines how much each service earns, so we run it as a checklist. We load perishable food at the commissary and check cold-chain temperatures before leaving. We drive to the service location with a realistic allowance for traffic, then set up the truck, connect to power when the site offers it and open for a lunch, dinner or event window. After service, we break down, clean on site and return to the commissary to wash equipment, empty gray water, dispose of grease properly and restock. That cycle easily fills ten to twelve hours of real work for a four-to-six-hour selling window, so when we plan the weekly route we favor stops that keep the drive between consecutive locations short and the line predictable. Our commissary and truck parking cost {{ocupacion_anual}} a year, a fixed cost we plan around every day we open.
81: Inventory is where a professional operator separates from a beginner, because almost everything on a truck is perishable and storage is tight. Buying daily or every other day takes more administrative effort, but it cuts spoilage and protects cash. In our plan, cost of goods is {{cogs_pct}} of sales, built on a food cost of {{food_cost_comida}} and a beverage cost of {{food_cost_bebida}}, with packaging and disposables adding {{consumibles_pct}} of sales. At {{clientes_dia}} customers a day and an average check of {{ticket}}, we sell about {{ventas_dia}} on an average opening day, which tells us how much product to buy and when to adjust. We keep opening inventory at {{inv_stock}} and set par levels for each item. We also keep at least two suppliers for each main category, so a missed delivery never closes the window for a day.
82: Preventive maintenance belongs on a written calendar, not in our heads. We schedule a regular mechanical inspection of the engine and brakes, monthly cleaning of hood filters and grease traps, periodic checks of the electrical system, propane lines and fire suppression, and routine replacement of wear items such as gaskets, belts and seals. Many jurisdictions require some of these checks to be documented, so the calendar doubles as inspection paperwork. We treat maintenance as a cost of doing business, never as an optional expense, because a breakdown in the middle of a service day costs more than the repair: lost sales, spoiled food and a customer who may not come back. That is also why our budget carries a cushion for repairs, and why the cash reserve in this plan is sized for surprises as well as for slow weeks.
85: Our staffing model has to balance production capacity against what the business can afford. With total startup investment of {{inversion_total}} and an average check of {{ticket}}, every hire has to pay for itself. A truck has to cover cooking, customer service, administration and driving at the same time, so we define each role clearly and set up our people policies to reduce our dependence on the owner without putting profitability at risk.
86: The minimum viable crew for a quality street-food truck is two or three people. The owner acts as chef and manager and is responsible for the food, quality control, finances, paperwork and getting the truck to the location. That concentration of roles keeps labor costs down but creates a real vulnerability: if the owner is sick or unavailable, the truck stops earning that day. Most trucks start this way, and we plan for it, but we also plan to add a second regular team member before volume makes it unavoidable. Our payroll in the example is {{plantilla_puestos}} people, or {{plantilla_jornadas}} full-time equivalents.
87: The cook and cashier supports daily service by prepping ingredients, assembling orders, handling the window and keeping the truck clean during the shift. At events with heavy crowds, such as festivals and busy markets, we bring in extra hands so that speed of service does not drop and quality stays where our regulars expect it. We can staff these peaks with part-time or seasonal employees or with a local staffing agency, which lets us match the crew to the seasonal swings of the business without carrying a full payroll all year.
88: Labor is the largest operating cost after food. In year 1 our labor cost is {{personal_a1}} including employer payroll taxes, or {{personal_pct}} of sales. We estimate payroll taxes at {{cargas_pct}} of wages, which covers the employer share of Social Security and Medicare, federal and state unemployment taxes and workers' compensation insurance; your actual rate depends on your state and insurer. Every wage we plan has to clear the legal floor: the federal minimum wage is $7.25 an hour, about {{salario_minimo_federal}} a year for a full-time position of {{horas_semana}} hours a week, and many states and cities set a higher minimum. Employees are hired on a W-2 and paid through payroll, while a 1099 contractor has to genuinely run their own business, so we do not use contractors for roles that we control, such as set shifts at our window. On top of wages, we budget uniforms, a meal during shifts and any travel to the location. Keeping this line under control is essential to reaching our target margins.
89: Training covers three areas. The first is speed: customers at a window expect their order in minutes, so how we organize the workspace and coordinate cooking and service sets how many people we can serve. The second is food safety: everyone who handles food needs a food handler card where the state or county requires one, and at least one certified food protection manager, for example through ServSafe, should be on the team. The crew also learns our HACCP-based food safety plan, temperature logs and allergen handling. The third is the physical routine of setting up and breaking down the truck, including power connections, awnings, propane safety and waste disposal, which can add up to an hour of unproductive time every day if the team is not practiced.
90: Managing people on a truck has its own quirks. Turnover is high across the food industry, so we hire for versatility and a willingness to learn as much as for experience. We plan vacations and replacements well in advance, because a truck that fails to show up at a booked event damages its reputation and loses revenue it cannot recover. We also keep timekeeping records for every employee, as the Fair Labor Standards Act requires. As demand grows, we add staff gradually and keep the cost structure under control, which is the most prudent path for a business of this size.
93: The economics of a food truck rest on a contained investment and a steady flow of customers, which is what makes the model so attractive within the restaurant business. A traditional restaurant typically demands a much larger commitment, a long lease and a bigger crew before it earns its first dollar. A truck lets us start smaller, test locations and menu, and recover capital faster, as long as we watch the numbers described below every week.
94: Total startup investment is {{inversion_total}}, of which {{capex}} goes into startup costs and {{fondo_maniobra}} into the working capital reserve. The cash we need at opening is {{necesidad_caja}}. The vehicle is the biggest item at {{inv_vehiculo}}, followed by {{inv_adaptacion}} for the build-out and wrap and {{inv_equipo_cocina}} for kitchen and refrigeration equipment. The generator adds {{inv_generador}}, first-year permits and licenses come to {{inv_permisos}}, opening inventory is {{inv_stock}}, and the launch marketing push costs {{inv_lanzamiento}}. We fund the project with {{fondos_propios}} of our own money, or {{aportacion_pct}} of the cash needed, and a {{prestamo}} bank or SBA 7(a) loan at {{tipo_prestamo}} nominal interest over {{plazo_prestamo}} years, with an annual payment of {{cuota_anual}} (annual equivalent; the lender will set monthly payments). It is the only debt in this plan, and the debt service coverage ratio is measured against it. The reserve is there to cover the slow early weeks while the truck builds its regulars.
95: Our revenue projection is built from the bottom up. In year 1 we expect {{ventas_a1}} in sales before sales tax, which works out to {{ventas_dia}} per opening day: {{clientes_dia}} customers at an average check of {{ticket}}, over {{dias}} days a year. In year 2, volume grows by {{crecimiento_a2}} to {{clientes_a2}} customers a day and revenue reaches {{ventas_a2}}. In year 3, with a further {{crecimiento_a3}} of growth, we serve {{clientes_a3}} customers a day and revenue reaches {{ventas_a3}}. Growth comes from regular lunch locations, repeat customers and larger events, not from raising prices.
96: Direct costs are in line with a quality quick-service concept. Cost of goods is {{cogs_pct}} of sales, which leaves a gross margin of {{margen_bruto_pct}}. Card processing fees take {{tarjeta_pct}} of sales, and labor costs {{personal_a1}} in year 1, or {{personal_pct}} of sales. Occupancy, meaning commissary and truck parking, adds {{ocupacion_anual}} a year, or {{ocupacion_pct}} of sales. Marketing is budgeted at {{marketing_anual}} a year. Total fixed costs in year 1 are {{costes_fijos_a1}}, including {{amortizacion_anual}} of depreciation and {{intereses_a1}} of loan interest. Insurance is {{seguros_anual}} a year.
97: Year-1 profit before income tax is {{resultado_antes_impuestos_a1}}, and EBITDA is {{ebitda_a1}}, or {{ebitda_pct_a1}} of sales. After income tax at an effective rate of {{impuesto_beneficios}} (a C corporation example; pass-through owners set it to 0 and pay tax on the profit personally), net profit is {{resultado_neto_a1}} in year 1, or a net margin of {{margen_neto_a1}}, rising to {{resultado_neto_a2}} in year 2 and {{resultado_neto_a3}} in year 3. Accounting break-even is {{equilibrio_clientes_dia}} customers a day, or {{equilibrio_ventas}} of revenue a year. Cash break-even (loan payments in, depreciation out) is {{equilibrio_caja_clientes_dia}} customers a day, or {{equilibrio_caja_ventas}} a year, so our margin of safety over cash break-even is {{holgura_caja_pct}}.
98: For the lender, the key figure is the debt service coverage ratio. In year 1 our DSCR is {{dscr_a1}}, and the lowest value over the life of the loan is {{dscr_min}}, compared with the {{dscr_objetivo}} that lenders typically look for. The workbook uses {{dscr_limite}} as its own warning limit. The lowest cash balance in year 1 is {{saldo_minimo}}, which you can trace on the "12-Month Cash Flow" tab and is the moment to watch most closely. Project payback before debt is {{payback}}, and payback on startup costs alone is {{payback_capex}}. These numbers show the plan is lender-ready, but approval is never guaranteed, and your own results will depend on your costs and locations.
99: The plan also has to survive a bad stretch. In the pessimistic scenario we serve {{pesimista_clientes}} customers a day at an average check of {{pesimista_ticket}} over {{pesimista_dias}} operating days, revenue is {{pesimista_ventas}} and the pre-tax result is {{pesimista_resultado}}. The estimated year-1 closing cash balance then falls to {{pesimista_caja}}: the working capital reserve would run out, so if sales track that case we cut costs or arrange extra funding well before it happens. In the optimistic scenario we serve {{optimista_clientes}} customers a day at {{optimista_ticket}} over {{optimista_dias}} days, revenue is {{optimista_ventas}} and the pre-tax result is {{optimista_resultado}}. The main risks are dependence on city permits for specific locations, growing competition among street-food concepts and volatile ingredient prices. We recommend agreements with several suppliers, a spread of locations and a base of corporate clients that generates recurring revenue through office catering.
102: Opening a food truck in the United States means working with several layers of government, and each one regulates something different. At the federal level, agencies such as the FDA set the food code model and labeling rules, and the IRS issues the employer identification number. The state typically handles business registration, sales tax and the health code the local departments enforce. Counties and cities usually issue the business license, the health permit and the vending permit. The U.S. Small Business Administration notes that state, county and city requirements depend on your activity and location, so we confirm each one with the local office before we spend money. A truck that sells in several cities has to complete this process in each one.
103: A mobile vending license is normally the first local requirement. It is issued by the city where we want to sell, and it is not transferable: a license in one city does not allow us to vend in another, and each truck needs its own. City ordinances also set where we can park, how long we can stay and how close we can be to restaurants, schools or other vendors, so we read the zoning and parking rules for every stop. To sell on private property, we get written permission from the owner. The City of Chicago, for example, publishes its own mobile food vendor license rules. Processing times vary widely, so we start these applications well before the planned opening.
104: The health permit for the truck is another pillar of compliance. In most jurisdictions the health department reviews the plans before we build or buy, and it will want to see the menu and equipment layout. Most require a signed commissary agreement showing where the truck stores food, takes on water and dumps waste, and the unit must pass an inspection before it opens. In Albuquerque, for example, the city requires a plan review, a signed commissary agreement and a separate permit for every mobile unit, and it notes that permits are not transferable. Requirements differ by county, so we check with our local health department before ordering any equipment.
105: Food safety rules mostly come from the state and county, but they are built on the FDA Food Code, which each state adopts in its own way. In most places we need at least one Certified Food Protection Manager, such as a ServSafe certificate, and food handler cards for the rest of the crew where the state or county requires them. Allergen labeling and communication matter too: federal law recognizes nine major food allergens, which are milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and, since 2023, sesame. We train the crew to answer allergen questions at the window and to avoid cross-contact.
106: Insurance is usually a condition of the permit and of event contracts. A food truck normally carries general liability insurance, because event organizers and property owners often ask for a certificate of insurance, commercial auto coverage for the vehicle and workers' compensation if we have employees, which almost every state requires. Some policies bundle these coverages. The example in this plan budgets {{seguros_anual}} a year for insurance, but quotes vary by state, driving record and coverage limits, so we collect several before we commit.
107: The vehicle itself carries legal requirements. The truck is registered and titled with the state motor vehicle agency, the DMV. Under federal rules (49 CFR 383.91), a commercial driver's license is required when the truck's gross vehicle weight rating is 26,001 pounds or more, or when it tows a trailer rated over 10,000 pounds and the combination is rated 26,001 pounds or more. Most food trucks can be driven with a regular license, but we check the rating on the door sticker before buying and confirm any extra state rules with the DMV. Fire safety is a separate step: in many cities the fire marshal inspects the propane system, fire extinguishers and hood suppression system, often before the health inspection, and NFPA 96 applies to cooking exhaust wherever it has been adopted. We also keep inspection records on board.
108: A truck that works in several locations has to plan for each one: every city can have its own license, and many require temporary food event permits for fairs, festivals and markets. Organizers usually ask for proof of insurance and our permits before they confirm a spot. The most practical strategy is to partner with event producers and market managers who already hold the right approvals, which simplifies the paperwork and reduces the risk of fines. A note for readers in the United Kingdom: register the food business with the local council at least 28 days before trading, which is free, and hold a street trading licence or consent from each council where the truck sells. Expect a hygiene inspection and a Food Hygiene Rating from 0 to 5 (England, Wales and Northern Ireland; Scotland uses the Food Hygiene Information Scheme), VAT at 20% on hot food and on food eaten on the premises, and 14 declared allergens.
111: A food truck is a way into the restaurant business with a controlled risk profile and real room to grow. Compared with a traditional restaurant, it needs a smaller investment, the learning curve is shorter, and mobility lets us test several locations before committing to a fixed address. With {{inversion_total}} of total startup investment and a year-1 pre-tax profit of {{resultado_antes_impuestos_a1}}, the plan lets us test the concept, generate cash and validate our assumptions before scaling into something more complex.
112: We see three main risks. The first is weather, which can cut revenue on rainy or very cold days. The second is the patchwork of permits, which differ from one city to the next and can take weeks or months to obtain. The third is dependence on one location or one power source. We reduce them with covered events, corporate catering and partnerships with indoor venues, and by starting permit applications as early as possible, working directly with each city and a local accountant or advisor who knows the licensing process. Our cash reserve of {{fondo_maniobra}} and a lowest year-1 cash balance of {{saldo_minimo}} show how much room we have to absorb a slow period.
113: Our strengths are operating flexibility and low fixed costs. We can be present at events, markets and busy zones without a long-term lease, and our commissary and parking cost {{ocupacion_anual}} a year. Social media is also a competitive advantage: a truck with a consistent content strategy builds a community of local followers that turns into repeat demand. The key is to show the preparation, show the ingredients and build a recognizable visual identity that sets us apart from the other trucks in each area. We plan to spend {{marketing_anual}} a year on marketing, with the launch push of {{inv_lanzamiento}} at the start.
114: Our roadmap follows the phases of the startup checklist included with this kit. In Phase 1 - Business Setup we form the company, register for taxes, obtain an EIN, open a business bank account and secure insurance. In Phase 2 - Truck & Permits we buy the vehicle, start the plan review with the health department, sign the commissary agreement and apply for the business license, health permit and vending permits. In Phase 3 - Equipment we build out the kitchen and install the generator, propane and fire suppression. In Phase 4 - Staff we hire, train and complete the payroll paperwork. In Phase 5 - Marketing we set up our social profiles, our Google Business Profile and the launch campaign, and in Phase 6 - First 90 Days we open with a small number of locations to learn which one earns the most per hour.
115: We track key performance indicators every week for the first six months. Customers per service show how well each location draws and whether it justifies the drive. Our target is {{clientes_dia}} customers a day. The average check, planned at {{ticket}}, tells us whether our prices and menu match the customer we aimed for. Sales per opening day, planned at {{ventas_dia}}, show real efficiency by tying income to the time we spend at each stop. Cost of goods against the planned {{cogs_pct}} and labor against {{personal_pct}} of sales tell us early if margins are slipping. The share of returning customers, which we measure with a simple QR loyalty program, shows how attached people are to the brand and how predictable our income can become.
116: Our medium-term vision has three horizons. In year 1 the goal is to reach break-even and to settle on a handful of recurring locations, with a margin of safety over cash break-even of {{holgura_caja_pct}}. In year 2, with volume up {{crecimiento_a2}}, we consider a second vehicle with a complementary concept, which would diversify the menu and win more corporate events and private parties. In year 3 we can evaluate a small fixed location that works as a flagship and prep kitchen, or a licensing model that lets others replicate the concept in other cities. Each step needs a hard look at our financing capacity, the availability of a qualified team and whether the local market can absorb the expansion without diluting our value proposition.
117: In the end, a food truck is a solid way into the restaurant business for people with operating experience, as long as the investment is planned carefully, the concept is clearly differentiated and the commitment to product quality and customer experience is firm. The plan shows total startup investment of {{inversion_total}}, funded with {{fondos_propios}} of our own money and a {{prestamo}} loan, and a project payback of {{payback}}. Our target customer is an urban consumer, roughly 20 to 45, with a medium-to-high income and the willingness to pay for a memorable meal. Replace the example numbers in the workbook with your own, review the legal checklist with your local authorities and your accountant, and bring the plan to the bank with confidence.
